questions.question:

questions.solution:

• **Example:** The curator organized a special exhibition on ancient Egyptian artifacts.

• Units of time, money, and distance are treated as a single collective unit and take a singular verb.

• "Advice" is an uncountable (mass) noun and must always be paired with a singular verb.

• **Passive Voice Rule:** To convert Simple Past to Passive, the structure used is "**was/were + past participle (V3)**".
 
• **Subject-Object Swap:** The object of the active sentence ("the plants") becomes the subject of the passive sentence.
 
• **Subject-Verb Agreement:** Since the new subject "the plants" is plural, we must use the auxiliary verb "**were**" instead of "was."
 
• **Consistency:** The frequency phrase "every morning" remains in its position to maintain the original meaning.

**Correct Sentence:** *"The plants were watered by the old woman every morning."*

Choose the correct indirect narration of the following statement from the given alternatives:

The lady said to her friend, "When was the bridge built here on this river?"

options.text: The lady asked her friend when the bridge had been built there on this river.
The lady asked her friend when the bridge had been built there on that river.
The lady asked her friend when the bridge was built there on that river.
The lady asked her friend when the bridge have been built there on that river.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Direct Speech:** The lady said to her friend, "When was the bridge built here on this river?"
 
• **Key Conversions:**
 
 
• **Reporting Verb:**
 
 
• The phrase **"said to"** changes to **"asked"** because the sentence is an interrogative (a question).
 
 
 
• **Tense Change (Simple Past to Past Perfect):**
 
 
• The simple past passive **"was built"** must be changed to the past perfect passive **"had been built"** because the reporting verb is in the past tense.
 
 
 
• **Words Expressing Nearness:**
 
 
• **"here"** changes to **"there"**.
 
• **"this"** changes to **"that"**.
 
 
 
• **Sentence Structure:**
 
 
• The question format (was the bridge built) changes to an assertive format (the bridge had been built). The question mark is replaced by a full stop.
 
 
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 2**.

 

**Correct Sentence:** *"The lady asked her friend when the bridge had been built there on that river."*

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1:** Incorrect because it fails to change "this" to "that."
 
• **Option 3:** Incorrect because it retains the simple past tense "was built" instead of back-shifting to the past perfect.
 
• **Option 4:** Incorrect because "have been built" is grammatically wrong in this context and is not a past perfect form.

questions.question:

He asked me what I was doing today.
He asked what I was doing today.

questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

• **Direct Speech:** He said, "What are you doing today?"
 
• **Key Conversions:**
 
 
• **Reporting Verb:**
 
 
• Since the sentence is a question, the reporting verb **"said"** is changed to **"asked"**.
 
 
 
• **Conjunction:**
 
 
• In "Wh-" questions, no external conjunction (like 'that' or 'if') is used. The question word **"what"** acts as the connector.
 
 
 
• **Pronoun Change:**
 
 
• The second-person pronoun **"you"** is changed based on the object of the reporting verb. Since no object is mentioned, it is common to assume the speaker is talking to "me," so "you" becomes **"I"**.
 
 
 
• **Tense Change (Present Continuous to Past Continuous):**
 
 
• The present continuous **"are doing"** changes to the past continuous **"was doing"** because the reporting verb is in the past tense.
 
 
 
• **Time Expression:**
 
 
• The word **"today"** is changed to **"that day"** in indirect speech.
 
 
 
• **Sentence Structure:**
 
 
• The interrogative form (Verb + Subject) is changed to an assertive form (Subject + Verb). Therefore, "are you doing" becomes "I was doing."
 
 
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**.

• **Option 4:** "He asked what I was doing today."

questions.question: Which of the following is a Fundamental Duty mentioned in the Indian Constitution?

options.text: To value the rich heritage of our composite ​culture
To not indulge in corrupt practices
To respect freedom of speech of others

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To value the rich heritage of our composite culture**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Fundamental Duties** were introduced in the Indian Constitution through the **42nd Amendment Act, 1976**, based on the recommendations of the **Swaran Singh Committee**. They are enshrined in **Article 51A**.
 
• One of the Fundamental Duties includes the obligation to **value and preserve the rich heritage of India’s composite culture**. This duty aims to inspire citizens to protect and promote India's diverse cultural legacy.
 
• The Fundamental Duties are applicable to **all Indian citizens**, and while they are not enforceable by law, they serve as a moral obligation to uphold the spirit of the Constitution.
 
• The statement “To value the rich heritage of our composite culture” is directly mentioned in **Article 51A(f)**, making it a part of the Fundamental Duties.
 
• Other duties include respecting the Constitution, promoting harmony, safeguarding public property, and striving for excellence, all of which aim to foster a sense of responsibility among citizens.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Fundamental Duties Overview:**

 
 
• There are currently **11 Fundamental Duties** listed under **Article 51A** of the Indian Constitution.
 
• These duties were inspired by the **Constitution of the USSR** and aim to promote patriotism and strengthen the unity of the nation.
 
• While these duties are non-justiciable, they complement Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy.
 
 
 
• **42nd Amendment Act, 1976:**
 
 
• The **42nd Amendment** is also known as the “Mini Constitution” due to the extensive changes it brought to the Indian Constitution.
 
• Besides introducing Fundamental Duties, it emphasized the importance of Directive Principles and strengthened the powers of the central government.
 
 
 
• **Preservation of Composite Culture:**
 
 
• India is known for its **diverse culture and heritage**, including monuments, art forms, languages, festivals, and traditions.
 
• The duty to preserve this heritage encourages citizens to actively participate in cultural preservation initiatives such as protecting historical sites and promoting cultural awareness.
 
• Examples include the **Clean India Campaign** to preserve heritage sites and cultural festivals such as **Surajkund Mela** and **International Yoga Day**.
 
 
 
• **Comparison with Fundamental Rights:**
 
 
• While **Fundamental Rights** are enforceable by the judiciary and provide protection to individuals, **Fundamental Duties** serve as moral obligations for citizens.
 
• Both aim to uphold the democratic framework of India and ensure the holistic development of society.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **List of Fundamental Duties:** **Article 51A** lists duties such as respecting the Constitution, cherishing national heritage, promoting harmony, and safeguarding public property.
 
• **Enforcement:** While Fundamental Duties are not legally enforceable, several initiatives like cultural education programs and civic awareness campaigns promote adherence.
 
• **Global Context:** Countries like **Japan** and **Russia** also emphasize citizen duties in their constitutions, highlighting the universal importance of moral obligations.
 
• **Civic Awareness:** Schools and colleges in India conduct programs to instill the importance of Fundamental Duties among students.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Prohibition** is a writ issued by a higher court, such as the **High Court or Supreme Court**, to prevent a lower court or tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction in hearing a case.
 
• This writ acts as a tool to ensure that judicial proceedings remain within the boundaries of the **legal authority** granted to the concerned judicial body.
 
• The writ of Prohibition is issued when a lower court or tribunal attempts to act beyond its jurisdiction or violates procedural laws.
 
• Prohibition is issued only to prevent an act from being done; it does not correct any action that has already been completed.
 
• It is a preventive measure and differs from other writs such as **Certiorari**, which is corrective in nature.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Writs in the Indian Constitution:**

 
 
• The Indian Constitution provides for five types of writs under **Article 32** (Supreme Court) and **Article 226** (High Courts).
 
• These writs are **Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari,** and **Quo Warranto**.
 
• These writs serve as tools to enforce fundamental rights and ensure judicial accountability.
 
 
 
• **Explanation of Other Writs:**
 
 
• **Habeas Corpus:** A writ issued to ensure the release of a person unlawfully detained. It protects the **personal liberty** of individuals.
 
• **Mandamus:** A writ directing a public authority to perform a duty it is legally obligated to fulfill.
 
• **Certiorari:** A writ issued to transfer a case from a lower court to a higher court or to quash an order passed by a lower court that exceeds its jurisdiction.
 
• **Quo Warranto:** A writ questioning the legality of a person's claim to a public office.
 
 
 
• **Key Characteristics of Prohibition:**
 
 
• **Jurisdictional Aspect:** Prohibition ensures that lower courts function within their legal jurisdiction.
 
• **Preventive Nature:** It prevents unlawful actions before they occur, unlike Certiorari, which corrects actions that have already happened.
 
• **Recipient:** It can only be issued to judicial and quasi-judicial bodies, not administrative authorities.
 
 
 
• **Examples:**
 
 
• Suppose a lower court decides to hear a matter related to international treaties, which is beyond its jurisdiction. The higher court can issue a writ of Prohibition to stop the proceedings.
 
• If a tribunal begins proceedings in violation of procedural rules laid down by statute, Prohibition can be issued to halt such proceedings.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Article 32 and Article 226:**

 
 
• While **Article 32** empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs for the enforcement of fundamental rights, **Article 226** gives similar powers to High Courts for both fundamental rights and other legal rights.
 
 
 
• **Judicial Review:** Prohibition is an integral part of the judicial review mechanism that ensures legal compliance and prevents abuse of power by lower courts and tribunals.
 
• **Limitations:** The writ cannot be issued against legislative bodies, private individuals, or administrative authorities acting in non-judicial capacities.

• **Observer States:**
 
 
• The SCO has several observer states, including **Afghanistan, Belarus, and Mongolia**, which participate in meetings but do not have voting rights.
 
 
 
• **Key Initiatives of SCO:**

• **Importance of SCO:**

• Before its establishment in **2001**, the organization functioned as the "**Shanghai Five**", which included China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Tajikistan.

__
 
• The light from the Sun takes approximately **8 minutes and 20 seconds** to travel the distance of about **149.6 million kilometers** (the average distance between the Sun and the Earth).
 
• This time is calculated based on the speed of light, which is approximately **299,792 kilometers per second** in a vacuum.
 
• Light travels at a finite speed, so the sunlight we see is slightly delayed, meaning we observe the Sun as it was about 8 minutes ago.
 
• The phenomenon is crucial for understanding astronomical observations, as light from distant celestial objects takes years, decades, or even centuries to reach Earth.
 
• The **8-minute travel time** is an average, as the distance between the Sun and Earth slightly varies due to the elliptical orbit of Earth around the Sun.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Speed of Light:**

 
 
• The speed of light in a vacuum is a constant and is approximately **299,792 kilometers per second** or **186,282 miles per second**.
 
• This value is a fundamental constant in physics and is denoted by the symbol **c**.
 
• It is the maximum speed at which all energy, matter, and information in the universe can travel.
 
 
 
• **Distance Between Sun and Earth:**
 
 
• The average distance from the Sun to Earth is referred to as an **Astronomical Unit (AU)** and is roughly equal to **149.6 million kilometers**.
 
• The actual distance varies throughout the year due to Earth's elliptical orbit, ranging from **147 million kilometers (perihelion)** to **152 million kilometers (aphelion)**.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Light Travel Time:**
 
 
• Light travel time helps astronomers determine the distance to celestial objects in space.
 
• For instance, the light from the Moon takes about **1.3 seconds** to reach Earth, while light from the closest star (other than the Sun), Proxima Centauri, takes about **4.24 years**.
 
 
 
• **Application in Astronomy:**
 
 
• The concept of light travel time allows scientists to observe the past states of celestial bodies, as we are essentially seeing them as they were when the light left them.
 
• This delay helps in studying the history and evolution of stars, galaxies, and the universe itself.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Light Year:** A light year is the distance that light travels in one year, approximately **9.46 trillion kilometers**. It is a unit often used to measure astronomical distances.
 
• **Solar Constant:** The energy received per unit area from the Sun at the top of Earth's atmosphere is known as the solar constant, approximately **1361 watts per square meter**.
 
• **Relativity of Time:** The finite speed of light is a cornerstone of Einstein's theory of relativity, implying that time and space are interlinked and relative to the observer's frame of reference.
 
• **Implications for Space Exploration:** Light travel time affects communication with spacecraft. For instance, signals from Mars take about **13 minutes** to reach Earth when the planets are at their farthest distance from each other.

• The **Attorney General of India** is the chief legal advisor to the Government of India and is appointed by the **President of India** under **Article 76** of the Constitution.
 
• The Attorney General holds office **during the pleasure of the President**. This means the tenure is not fixed and depends solely on the President's discretion.
 
• The Attorney General has the right to participate in the proceedings of both Houses of Parliament but **does not have voting rights**.
 
• The Attorney General is responsible for advising the government on legal matters and performing other legal duties assigned by the President.
 
• Unlike other constitutional functionaries, such as the **Chief Justice of India** or **Comptroller and Auditor General**, the Attorney General does not enjoy security of tenure, as they serve at the President's pleasure.
 
• **Hence, the Attorney General of India holds office during the pleasure of the President of India.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• Appointed under **Article 148** of the Indian Constitution, the CAG is responsible for auditing accounts of the government and public sector organizations.
 
• The CAG enjoys security of tenure and cannot be removed from office except through a process similar to the impeachment of a Supreme Court judge.
 
• The CAG does not hold office during the pleasure of the President.

• The CJI is appointed by the President under **Article 124** of the Constitution and is the head of the judiciary system in India.
 
• The CJI serves until the age of **65 years** and cannot be arbitrarily removed by the President, ensuring independence.
 
• The Chief Justice does not hold office during the pleasure of the President.
 
 
 
• **Chief Election Commissioner (CEC):**
 
 
• Appointed under **Article 324** of the Constitution, the CEC oversees free and fair elections in India.
 
• The CEC enjoys security of tenure and can only be removed in the manner prescribed for Supreme Court judges.
 
• The Chief Election Commissioner does not hold office during the pleasure of the President.
 
 
 
• **Function of the Attorney General:**
 
 
• The Attorney General represents the Government of India in legal cases before the Supreme Court and High Courts.
 
• They can take part in parliamentary debates and discussions and advise the government on constitutional and legal matters.
 
• The Attorney General is not considered a government servant and can engage in private practice, provided it does not conflict with their duties.
 
• The position of Attorney General is modeled after the British system, where the Attorney General serves as the chief legal adviser to the Crown.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

• The Attorney General does not have a fixed tenure and can be removed or replaced at any time by the President.
 
• This flexible arrangement ensures that the Attorney General remains aligned with the government's priorities and policies.
 
 
 
• **Legal Framework:**
 
 
• Articles **74, 76, and 88** of the Constitution define the role and powers of the Attorney General.
 
• The Attorney General's primary responsibility is to maintain the government's legal integrity and represent it in judicial matters.
 
 
 
• **Eligibility Criteria:**
 
 
• The Attorney General must be qualified to be appointed as a judge of the Supreme Court, requiring a minimum of **five years of experience as a High Court judge** or **10 years of legal practice**.

• **Pineal Gland:**
 
 
• The pineal gland is a small endocrine gland located in the brain and is responsible for the production of the hormone **melatonin**.
 
• Melatonin regulates sleep-wake cycles but does not influence puberty in females.
 
 
 
• **Hypothalamus:**
 
 
• The hypothalamus is a part of the brain that regulates various hormonal processes by releasing **gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)**.
 
• GnRH stimulates the pituitary gland to release LH and FSH, which in turn stimulate the ovaries. While essential, the hypothalamus itself does not release puberty-specific hormones directly.
 
 
 
• **Ovaries:**
 
 
• The ovaries are the primary endocrine glands responsible for the hormonal changes associated with puberty in human females.
 
• They produce **estrogen**, which triggers the development of secondary sexual characteristics and prepares the body for reproduction.

• **Role of Estrogen:**

 
 
• Estrogen is essential for the development of primary and secondary sexual characteristics such as breast enlargement, fat distribution in hips and thighs, and the growth of the endometrial lining in the uterus.
 
• This hormone also regulates the menstrual cycle and supports reproductive health.
 
 
 
• **Age of Puberty:**
 
 
• Puberty in females generally begins between the ages of **8 and 13**, with significant hormonal changes occurring during this time.
 
 
 
• **Menstrual Cycle:**
 
 
• The ovaries play a critical role in the menstrual cycle by releasing eggs and producing hormones like estrogen and progesterone that regulate the cycle.
